Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

content.text: ~15,200 probes run. The split_path algorithm itself survived everything; clause 9 (what it receives) broke.

counterexamples.predictedByRule: 3 (rule says '#' only removes a trailing fragment, so a reader applying clause 9 to the URL's fragment component gets scheme='a/b/c', authority='e.com', path='' -> 0 segments; conversely the rule's clause 1 claims '#' changes the count *only* via fragment stripping, which cannot INCREASE a count) — the rule is self-contradictory here: the fragment-component reading predicts 0, and no reading in the rule predicts an increase from 0
counterexamples.actual: 3 segments [a, b, c]. Baseline 'a/b/c://e.com' => 0 segments. Inserting '#' RAISES the count 0 -> 3, because parse truncates the WHOLE input at the first '#' *before* it looks for '://', so 'a/b/c' never becomes a scheme and instead becomes the entire path.

counterexamples.predictedByRule: 2 segments [a, b] — clause 9 says only the fragment (from the first '#') is removed by parse and split_path gets URL::path(); with scheme 'ht#tp'/authority 'e.com' the path is '/a/b'
counterexamples.actual: 1 segment [ht]. The '#' cut is global and pre-scheme, so the surviving string is 'ht', which contains no '://' and therefore becomes the whole path.

counterexamples.predictedByRule: 2 segments [a, b] (same reasoning: '#' inside the scheme is not a fragment delimiter for the path component)
2 segments [a, b] — first '?' should only cut a query off the path
counterexamples.actual: 1 segment [x]; the '?' truncates the whole URL string before '://' is searched for

input.correctedRule:
split_path(p) is a pure, byte-oriented split of its input string on the single ASCII byte '/' (0x2F), discarding every empty piece. Nothing else: no trimming, no percent-decoding, no normalization, no case folding, no dedup, no dot-segment handling, no other separator, no length or count cap.

Exact algorithm (implementable verbatim, unchanged from the proposal — this part is fully confirmed):

  fn split_path(p: &[u8]) -> Vec<Vec<u8>> {
      let mut out = Vec::new();
      let mut cur: Vec<u8> = Vec::new();
      for &b in p {
          if b == b'/' {                 // 0x2F is the ONLY separator
              if !cur.is_empty() { out.push(std::mem::take(&mut cur)); }
          } else {
              cur.push(b);
          }
      }
      if !cur.is_empty() { out.push(cur); }
      out
  }

Equivalently: `p.split('/').filter(|s| !s.is_empty()).map(String::from).collect()`.

=== CONFIRMED PROPERTIES OF split_path ITSELF ===

1. Separator set = exactly {0x2F}. Every byte 1..=255 was placed both as a lone segment (`/X/z`) and inside a segment (`/aXb`): only 0x2F changed the segment count. Backslash 0x5C, ';', ':', '@', ',', '=', '&', '[', ']', 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x7F are all ordinary segment bytes. (0x23 '#' and 0x3F 0x3F '?' also change the count, but that is a URL::parse effect — see section B, and note the mechanism is NOT what the proposal said.)

2. NO trimming whatsoever, despite the existence of an internal trim(). Whitespace-only segments SURVIVE and are counted: `/ /` -> 1 [" "]; `/   ` -> 1 ["   "]; `/ a / b /` -> 2 [" a ", " b "]; `/a/ /b` -> 3 ["a", " ", "b"]; `/\t/\x0b/\r/\x0c/ /\xff` -> 6 single-byte segments. Only literally-empty pieces are dropped.

3. NO url_decode anywhere in this pipeline, for ANY percent form. Verified literal pass-through of: %41, %2F, %2f, %252F, %%2F, %2, bare %, %00, %0A, %09, %20, %2B, %3F, %3f, %23, %25, %7E, %2E%2E, %c3%a9, %C3%A9, %ff, %u002F, and '+' . Critically %2F/%2f are NOT separators (`/a%2Fb` -> 1 ["a%2Fb"]), and %3F/%23 are NOT query/fragment delimiters (`/a%3Fb?c` -> 1 ["a%3Fb"]). '+' is never turned into a space.

4. NO dot-segment removal, NO dedup, NO reordering: `/./ /..` -> 3 [".", " ", ".."]; `/a/a/a/a` -> 4; `/./../a` -> 3 [".", "..", "a"].

5. Empty / all-separator inputs give 0 segments: "" -> 0; "/" -> 0; "///" -> 0; 1000 '/' -> 0.

6. Leading/trailing '/' contribute nothing; runs of '/' collapse. Relative and absolute paths behave identically: "a/b/c" and "/a/b/c" -> 3; "//a/b" and "a//b" -> 2; "/a//" -> 1.

7. Total byte transparency. All 252 argv-passable bytes (1..255 minus 0x2F/0x23/0x3F) round-trip byte-for-byte in every position tested (lone segment, doubled, interior), verified by exact raw-output comparison, not by eyeballing. No UTF-8 awareness or validation: lone 0x80, 0xFF, 0xA0, 0x85 and truncated UTF-8 prefixes are preserved verbatim. Embedded 0x0A and 0x0D are ordinary bytes and are emitted verbatim, which makes the line-oriented driver output ambiguous — the LINE 5 count is the authoritative segment count, not the number of trailing lines.

8. Output order is input order. The count prints as a plain decimal integer with no locale grouping, and this is locale-INDEPENDENT: with LC_ALL/LANG set to C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8 and POSIX, 12345 segments always prints "12345". No caps: 65 000 segments all emitted and counted exactly; a single segment of 131 050 bytes is emitted byte-exact. The only wall is the OS argv limit (MAX_ARG_STRLEN = 131 072): a 131 073-byte argv fails with exit 127 / E2BIG before the program runs. Byte 0x00 remains untestable through argv (execve terminates the string), so NUL handling is inferred, not observed.

=== CORRECTED SECTION B: WHAT split_path ACTUALLY RECEIVES ===

The proposal's clause 9 is wrong/incomplete. It is NOT true that "the query (from the first '?') and fragment (from the first '#') are already removed by parse" in the sense of URL *components*. The cut is GLOBAL and happens BEFORE scheme/authority detection. The observed derivation of URL::path() is:

  cut  = min(index of first '?', index of first '#') over the ENTIRE input string (or end of string if neither occurs)
  s    = input[0 .. cut)                       // everything from the first '?' or '#' onward is discarded outright
  i    = index of the first occurrence of "://" in s
  if i >= 0:  rest = s[i+3 ..];  j = index of first '/' in rest
              path = (j >= 0) ? rest[j ..] : ""      // authority is rest[0..j); '/' is the ONLY authority terminator left
  else:       path = s                                // no "://" => the whole (already-truncated) string is the path
  segments = split_path(path)

Consequences the proposal missed, all observed:
  - A '?' or '#' anywhere — including inside what looks like the scheme, or before the "://" — truncates the whole URL and can therefore turn an absolute URL into a relative path. 'ht#tp://e.com/a/b' -> 1 ["ht"], not 2 ["a","b"]. 'http#://e.com/a/b' -> 1 ["http"]. 'x?y/http://e.com/a/b' -> 1 ["x"].
  - Because of that, adding a '?' or '#' can INCREASE the segment count, not just decrease it: 'a/b/c://e.com' -> 0 segments, but 'a/b/c#://e.com' and 'a/b/c?://e.com' -> 3 ["a","b","c"]. Likewise '/a/b://e.com/zzz' -> 1 ["zzz"] vs '/a/b#://e.com/zzz' -> 2 ["a","b"].
  - Whether '?' or '#' is removed "first" is unobservable and irrelevant: the net effect is a single cut at the earlier of the two ('/a?b#c/d', '/a#b?c/d', '/a#b/c?d', '/a?b/c#d' all -> 1 ["a"]).
  - The "://" match is the FIRST occurrence: 'a://b://c/d/e' -> authority 'b:', path '//c/d/e' -> 3 ["c","d","e"]; 'http://e.com://x/y' -> 2 ["x","y"]; 'http:://e.com/a/b' -> scheme 'http:' (invalid), path '/a/b' -> 2.
  - Only a literal "://" starts the authority; ':/' does not ('http:/e.com' -> 2 ["http:", "e.com"]) and percent-encoded forms do not ('http%3A%2F%2Fe.com/a/b' -> 3 ["http%3A%2F%2Fe.com","a","b"], 'http:%2F%2Fe.com/a/b' -> 3).
  - Backslash does NOT terminate the authority: 'http://e.com\a\b' -> host 'e.com\a\b' (invalid), path "" -> 0 segments.
  - The '/' bytes consumed by parse (the two in "://" and the one that terminates the authority) are not seen by split_path; "the only separator is '/'" is a statement about split_path's input, not about the URL string.
  - No whole-string trim: '  http://e.com/a  ' -> scheme "  http" (invalid), host 'e.com' (valid), 1 segment "a  ". Trailing space/tab/CR/LF/VT/FF/0xA0 are all kept in the last segment; a leading one always invalidates the scheme.

With that corrected path-derivation model, 14 000 randomized inputs over an alphabet including '/', '?', '#', ':', '%', '+', '\\', space, TAB, CR, LF, VT, FF, 0xA0, 0xC3, 0xA9, 0xE2, 0x80, 0xFF matched the binary's raw output byte-for-byte with zero mismatches.
input.notes:
~15,200 probes total: a 504-probe full byte sweep (every byte 1..255 in two positions), a 504-probe exact byte-fidelity sweep (raw-output equality, not eyeballing), 14,000 randomized differential-fuzz probes against reference implementations, plus ~200 hand-built targeted probes (percent-encoding variants, whitespace, locale, size/cap boundaries, delimiter-ordering, authority boundaries).

From my assigned lens (decoding and byte preservation) the rule is IMPECCABLE — I could not dent it. Every decoding claim held: 20+ distinct percent forms including %2F/%2f/%252F/%3F/%23/%00/%u002F pass through literally, '+' is never a space, and no byte of output is ever anything but a verbatim copy of an input byte. Byte preservation held for all 252 argv-passable bytes in every position, verified by exact raw-string comparison. I also killed two of the three flagged uncertainties: the count formatting is locale-independent (tested C/C.UTF-8/en_US/de_DE/tr_TR/POSIX), and the size ceilings are purely the OS argv limit — 65,000 segments and a 131,050-byte single segment both work perfectly, while 131,073 bytes of argv fails with E2BIG (exit 127) before main() runs, so there is no library-side cap. NUL genuinely cannot be reached through argv; I confirmed there is no percent-decode path that could smuggle one in, so it stays inferred.

The break is in clause 9, the one clause that describes what split_path receives rather than what it does. The proposal says parse removes "the query (from the first '?') and fragment (from the first '#')", which reads as component-wise stripping. In reality the truncation is global and happens BEFORE the "://" search, so a '?' or '#' sitting in the scheme (or anywhere left of "://") destroys the scheme/authority split entirely. The sharpest demonstration is that a '#' can RAISE the segment count, which the proposal's clause 1 framing ("'#' and '?' change the count only because parse strips the fragment/query") implicitly forbids: 'a/b/c://e.com' gives 0 segments, 'a/b/c#://e.com' gives 3 ["a","b","c"]. Two implementers reading clause 9 would disagree on all five counterexamples, so this is a 'corrected' rather than 'confirmed'.

Also worth flagging as an output-format caveat the rule is silent on: because 0x0A is preserved verbatim inside a segment, the driver's line-oriented output is ambiguous for such inputs ('http://e.com/a' + LF prints "a" then an empty line for a single 1-count segment). The LINE 5 count, not the trailing line count, is authoritative.
